extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house IP counsel, patentees, and stakeholders involved in U.S. patent prosecution and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and cautionary standards for filing, defending, and responding to terminal disclaimers in U.S. patent prosecution, including current practice, relevant case law, USPTO policy (MPEP), and proposed rule changes that affect enforceability of patents tied by terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer effect on patent expiration date
rubrics_metrics.description: In a terminal disclaimer, the patent applicant is agreeing that the patent issuing from the application being prosecuted will have the expiration date of the reference patent or a patent issuing from the reference application (if the ODP rejection is based on a pending application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a terminal disclaimer ties expiration to the reference patent, the resulting patent can expire earlier than it otherwise would have; patentees should understand that the disclaimer changes the patent term. See also discussion that terminal disclaimers are part of the original patent and give public notice (35 U.S.C. § 253).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership requirement in terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent applicant agrees that any patent issuing from the patent application being prosecuted, and the reference patent or a patent issuing from the reference application, will have common ownership during their common patent term (or in the case of a joint research agreement, common enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because enforceability is conditioned on common ownership (or common enforcement under a joint research agreement), applicants must ensure the referenced patent is in fact commonly owned; failure can render the disclaimed patent unenforceable, as illustrated by the SIPCO case where the referenced patent was never owned by the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability contingent on continued common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional agreement in a terminal disclaimer is that any patent issuing from the application and the reference patent will only be enforceable during the common patent term so long as the two patents are commonly owned (or in the case of a joint research agreement, commonly enforced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may hold patentee to the plain language of the disclaimer and treat the patent as unenforceable if the common-ownership condition is not met at issuance or thereafter; in SIPCO the court held the erroneous terminal disclaimer rendered the patent unenforceable upon issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous terminal disclaimer cannot be cured by reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The erroneous filing of a terminal disclaimer cannot be cured by a reissue application, see Ex parte Yamazaki, Appeal 2010-002033 (BPAI 2011), aff’d, In re Yamazaki, 702 F.3d 1327 (Fed. Cir. 2012) (overruling Ex parte Durckheimer, Appeal 94-2004 (BPAI 1996)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reissue will not remedy an erroneous terminal disclaimer, an inadvertent or mistaken disclaimer can have permanent, incurable consequences for a patentee. Practitioners must therefore be careful when filing a terminal disclaimer and verify the correctness of referenced patents/applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO post‑grant policy on withdrawing incorrect terminal disclaimers (MPEP 1490(VIII)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO updated the MPEP (effective Aug. 15, 2017) to provide that the USPTO will not, after a patent has been granted, withdraw an incorrect terminal disclaimer that was the result of an inadvertent error, but rather will only allow a patentee to put on file an explanation of the error and additional terminal disclaimer(s) that may correct the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions to withdraw an incorrect terminal disclaimer post-grant are generally dismissed; the available remedy is to file explanatory material and additional terminal disclaimers, which may not restore enforceability or prevent adverse effects. See the October 20, 2017 petition decision in the USPTO file for the ’304 patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from transcription errors and need for practitioner diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcription errors (e.g., referencing the wrong patent number) can lead to filing a terminal disclaimer over an unintended reference patent, producing avoidable and severe consequences (the SIPCO example: terminally disclaiming over U.S. Patent No. 6,430,267 when the intended reference was 6,430,268).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent practitioners have an onus to diligently review the conflicting patents and/or pending applications cited in an obviousness‑type double patenting (ODP) rejection to determine whether the rejection is proper and the correct reference is identified; however, USPTO transcription errors can still leave patentees vulnerable under current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and futility of corrective standalone terminal disclaimers after adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a standalone terminal disclaimer over the correct reference after discovery of an error may not remedy prior adverse outcomes (e.g., the ’304 patent had already expired based on a terminal disclaimer as to yet another patent, and a later-filed standalone terminal disclaimer over the intended patent did not fix the enforceability problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because post‑grant corrections may come too late to prevent expiry or unenforceability, early detection and correction during prosecution is critical. Do not rely on later standalone disclaimers to reverse harms caused by an earlier, erroneous disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimers are part of the original patent and provide public notice (35 U.S.C. § 253)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimers, upon taking effect, are considered part of the original patent and assist in providing public notice as to the full scope of the limited monopoly granted to the patentee by the patent system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given their role in public notice, patentees are held to the promises in executed terminal disclaimers; courts will construe and enforce their plain language to protect the public from harassment by multiple assignees or unexpected patent term extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed USPTO rule: unenforceability if tied (directly or indirectly) to a patent with invalidated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's May 10, 2024 proposed rule would require applicants, upon filing a terminal disclaimer to obviate ODP, to agree that the underlying patent is enforceable only if the patent 'is not, and has never been, tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting where any claim has been invalidated under anticipation or obviousness by the USPTO or federal court or statutorily disclaimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the proposed rule, if a reference patent (directly tied) has a claim invalidated over prior art, patents tied via terminal disclaimers could become unenforceable. This expands risk and ties enforceability to the validity of other patents in the chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain‑reaction risk from indirect links via series of terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents and co‑pending applications within a patent family may be indirectly linked together based on a series of terminal disclaimers identifying other family members as reference applications or patents; in this scenario, a patent family that is tied directly and indirectly together by a series of terminal disclaimers risks being unenforceable in its entirety if one claim in any one patent is invalidated over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners and stakeholders should evaluate not only direct terminal disclaimers but also the network of terminal disclaimers that may indirectly link family members. The proposed rule could cause a chain reaction wiping out entire patent families, even when disputed subject matter is distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed rules exacerbate harms from USPTO or human error and reduce post‑grant recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Because current procedures generally do not permit withdrawal of erroneous terminal disclaimers post-grant, the proposed rules, by expanding grounds for unenforceability across linked patents, would further disserve the public and patentees and could leave patentees with no recourse for USPTO transcription or human error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments on the proposed rule are a practical avenue for stakeholders to seek changes (comment deadline noted). In the interim, patentees should be cautious when executing terminal disclaimers and consider procedural strategies during prosecution to minimize downstream risks.
